comments.author: nik_s
comments.text: I think the layman's perception of the increase in survival (~13 months versus ~6 months) will make this look underwhelming. Nevertheless, it's important to remember that the incentives for clinical trials is to only include very late-stage patients who have exhausted all other options (faster trials, smaller sample sizes, surrogate endpoints, a shot at accelerated approval, ...). The fact that a treatment shows promise for these patients that are often in very poor health and considered "hopeless" by today's medicine is exceedingly rare, and the signal from this trial is indeed strong. The (somewhat reasonable) hope is that patients 1. with earlier forms of pancreatic cancer (non-metastatic) 2. that can undergo surgery 3. together with a (neo)adjuvant treatment with these kras inhibitors, will end up having a much lower recurrence rate and a chance for a long, healthy life. I think this is genuinely good news worth celebrating!

comments.author: mft_

It won’t cure people with metastatic disease, but it will help a lot live better lives for longer.

comments.author: rcr-anti
comments.text: While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now. Following a few bugs and bad proofs this year, there are a number of different implementations, in different languages, and with different levels of proofs of their consistency. con-leche and con-ron are the heavy hitters, with consistency proofs of themselves. So for RH to be false, there'd have to be a bug in all the kernels that affects both the consistency proofs and the RH proof itself.

comments.author: thejokeisonme
comments.text: A fake refutation of the Collatz conjecture already got through one of these independent checkers in the past. What's harder, proving GRH or finding a way to get through every checker (which aren't as independent as they are sometimes touted to be)? In this case there was a human expert in the loop so it's much less likely the model hacked its way through the problem without the expert noticing. But the statement as written has 4 points, none of which rests on the human involvement. So I don't like that they claim full confidence based on those points.

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text: If you're new to quantized models: Don't get too excited about claims of fitting large models into tiny RAM footprints from random GitHub repos. There is always a tradeoff, and it's too easy to benchmaxx KL-divergence numbers and even single benchmark scores. Just because you can get something to run on a device doesn't mean it's going to be useful. The headline claim of this repo (12X better) doesn't even apply to Inkling-2-Mini This repo's README is a mess of different histories as the author bounces from one popular model to the next. It refers to vague things like "the 1.2GB file" that probably made sense in an early vibecoding pass, but are now lost after the repo has been pushed around to different popular models. The truth is that random GitHub repos with messy READMEs almost never hold a real secret that the mainstream quantizations have missed. I would recommend sticking to mainstream quantizations like the official GGML release, Unsloth's quants, or the more well known community quantizers like bartowski or AesSedai. They typically follow an optimized size-quality tradeoff so you can find the one that fits your needs. When you see a repo like this where everything is so obviously vibecoded that the README is a rambling mix of projects and claims, you should probably go looking for a more authoritative source. The local LLM communities get spammed with 10 of these types of projects per day but I have yet to see a real breakthrough come from any of the vibecoded ones. The real work is coming from people who study this and have compute to test at scale or work on implementing advanced techniques which require inference engine support, like trellis quants.

comments.author: senko
comments.text: This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3. At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows. End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours. (For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)

comments.author: fancyfredbot
comments.text: Since lots of comments misunderstood the article, the extra latency from going through the monitor meant his laptop couldn't acknowledge the packets quickly enough. That led a buffer on the ethernet adapter to fill and that led it to drop packets. A different adapter which required less frequent acknowledgement fixed the problem for him. It is quite a nice post which gets to the bottom of incredibly opaque behaviour of USB hubs.

comments.author: __benny__
comments.text: Nice article, thank you for sharing it. I do want to nitpick this part however: > That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor. It's a common criticism but I don't think it's based on anything other than preconceived notions about rendering being slow and doing a ton of caching makes everything faster. but neither seem to be backed up by any sort of empirical evidence. Anecdotally every imgui I've used has been lightening fast, and retained mode UI's like the browser, windows software, new Macos apps written in SwiftUI, etc, have performance problems. Egui has solved the accessibility problem and does a lot of caching: galleys, glyphs, and layouts are cached, packed texture atlases minimize GPU uploads, and it uses inputs & animation state to draw on demand. I also don't see how retained mode UI would scale better. Retained mode UI's are typically slow - they have a complex multi-pass general layout system and a ton of bookkeeping, which is why you typically need to keep updates to a minimum and ever-more-complex change tracking systems are being built to reduce updates to a minimum. This doesn't scream scalability to me - whereas in an imgui there is a baseline overhead but adding more widgets or more frequent updates have a negligible performance impact. the worst case for retained mode is a UI which has many widgets frequently updating multiple times a second, which means you approach the update and drawing of imgui but with the additional overhead of the change tracking, bookkeeping, etc of the retained system. Also there is nothing fundamental about imgui layout systems being limited, and in my experience it's not that difficult to build custom widgets to implement pretty much anything. Retained mode layout systems are usually declarative, where you describe a layout and hope that the system is flexible enough to support what you want, whereas with an imgui you can just directly draw and shade geometry to get whatever you want. Otherwise, great article and I look forward to the future of Rust UI.

comments.text: Seems pretty promising in a few quick coding tests. 27 tokens/s decode on Ryzen 395 and llama.cpp Vulkan. Besides the obvious unmerged PRs (32694, 32657, 32429, 32704) you'll want below tiny patch for about 30% speed boost. Also, if anyone from the team is reading, if you have access for researchers I'd be interested in doing some higher volume tests & harness tuning than I have hardware for personally. --- a/src/llama-graph.cpp +++ b/src/llama-graph.cpp @@ -2670,10 +2670,12 @@ ggml_tensor \* llm_graph_context::build_moe_ffn( const float beta = hparams.situ_beta; const float lb = hparams.situ_linear_beta; - ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, cur, 1.0f/beta)), beta); + // gate/up are strided views of the fused gate_up output; ggml-vulkan's SCALE + // needs a contiguous src, so without the cont both scales fall back to the CPU + ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, cur), 1.0f/beta)), beta); act = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, ggml_sigmoid(ctx0, cur)); if (lb > 0.0f) { - up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, up, 1.0f/lb)), lb); + up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, up), 1.0f/lb)), lb); } cur = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, up); cb(cur, "ffn_moe_situ", il);

comments.text: C# already provides many tools for your performance-critical code though. You can use pointers in unsafe. You can allocate unmanaged memory with Marshal. You can avoid copy with Span. You can even manually vectorise with Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated and such. You can also distribute apps without .NET runtime with NativeAOT. I'm sure there are people who want a C# without GC, but for me it's just... sufficient enough.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text: The GC is a feature. Not a bug to be eliminated. GC is not surrendering control. That seems to be HN's #1 bug bear. The sensation that someone or something is taking control away from you. The proper way to frame this is that you can actually focus on the original problem you set out to solve. Risking memory leaks is crazy when it's not something the customer is demanding. Even in gaming I think the GC is fine. There are ways to spread the impact across frames and bound the amount of time spent collecting. If your clever scheme wouldn't work with a GC-managed heap, it probably won't work with one managed by hand either.

comments.author: YuechenLi
comments.text: So... What does this have over using NativeAOT which already exists? Keep in mind a large portion of time NativeAOT is actually SLOWER than going through RyuJIT with the only definitive benefit being smaller binaries, and it's not like you can't do Span<T> and ref structs in modern C# for manual low level memory control already. So my question is just... why?

comments.author: andix
comments.text: Assuming this is very similar to bflat: it's a cool idea and fun to play with, but not very useful. C# is not designed to run without a GC, existing code usually won't run, because the standard library is missing. Just using C, Rust, Zig, or whatever is probably nearly always the better option. Those languages are designed to work without GC and provide various well established ways to manage memory.

comments.author: hollowonepl
comments.text: I’m not sure, the whole point of this language, standard libraries and runtime is built around GC. Nobody from C# world is educated or prepared to manually manage memory. This is just bare metal C++ with a lot of it stripped away and just nicer/cleaner syntax that does not inherit so much from C and POSIX archeology. Nice POC, especially on MS-DOS but nothing truly relevant in the long run, I’m afraid

comments.author: khaliostr
comments.text: There's a bit of an open source Magic renaissance going on lately, which I find really cool. Forge has been around forever, but we've managed to get it running in the browser via WASM with Manabrew [1]. I'm one of the maintainers, and we're mostly building it because we wanted a nicer way to play Commander with friends. Meanwhile, Phase and Ironsmith are working on new engines in Rust, Gorge is building one in Go alongside a bot and cross-engine testing tools, and people are starting to collaborate across projects. I note that Fable 5.2 improved our throughput on game engine mechanics and playable cards dramatically (mostly through redesigning processes), but I worry the Anthropic and OpenAI models will crap out when I begin asking them to help out with RL. comments.author: hannob
comments.text: It's been known for a while, and certainly long before the recent AI vuln flood, that ghostscript is really problematic in terms of security. Ultimately, postscript is its own programming language, and executing a programming language in a secure, sandboxed way is not trivial. ghostscript has only a very poor pseudo sandbox that fails regularly. Unfortunately, ghostscript is the only implementation of postscript that's out there. All of that would matter much less if people only used it to parse postscript. But it's used indirectly by imagemagick (you can disable it), which means many people using imagemagick to parse images from untrusted sources get exposed to ghostscript's poor security.

comments.author: powvans
comments.text: > In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. I don't know the OP's circumstances. What I am about to say is meant as advice to others and not a criticism of the OP. If you suspect that you may be the target of a layoff, DO NOT SIMPLY QUIT. In this scenario you are a potential liability to your employer. They will almost certainly pay you to leave if they decide to part ways. It is always easier to find a job when you have a job. Maybe you think if there are layoffs and you are retained that it will be a miserable working environment. Fine. DO NOT QUIT. After a round of layoffs you are relatively safe and you can use that time to find another job. It is very likely that layoffs are going to continue as companies restructure because of AI. Have a plan. Keep your wits and hold fast.

comments.author: imeanwhatdoikno
comments.text: There's a short comment elsewhere here that says "you need to lie" which basically summarizes it. To expand on that: you need to tell potential employers about your AI-powered SaaS or whatever startup that you've been working on for the past two years, how much you accomplished just by yourself with the help AI agents, how much you learned about using AI effectively, etc. That you just couldn't get enough traction in sales and funding and the area you addressed is now being broadly up-ended by AI, so you are looking for a more regular job On the side you obviously need a demo of what you've built over these two years, but Claude can help with both brainstorming what your startup actually did and building it retroactively. In the process it will force you to actually start using AI for real which will be a nice bootstrap for your eventual real job.

comments.author: taurath
comments.text: I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.

comments.author: neoCrimeLabs
comments.text: Something I expect from a senior engineer is the ability to take a failure without placing blame, and turn it into an opportunity to improve things while also taking actions to prevent the same failure mode from occuring. Gaps on resumes are not unique to you. People have unexpected unemployment for many reasons. If you treat that gap like it's a negative thing, and as you say "explain it", I'm going to think there's something negative behind it. Instead treat it as a matter of fact, then present the opportunities you took in the mean time. What makes someone with a gap stand out to is how they "sell" that gap to me. What did you do in that time to improve yourself, keep your skills sharp, grow as a human being? How are you going to show me that you still have passion and drive to remain in this industry? Also, reframe your thinking. You are not an engineer looking for work, you are a sales person selling an engineer. Take time to understand what qualities in an engineer they want beyond mere skills and experience. For example, you don't sell a used car by starting with "It's been on the road 15 years". You try to appeal to what the buyer is looking for. Do they want an easily customizable sports car, a reliable commuter, fuel efficiency? Hiring teams are buyers, you're the product. There's a lot of other boring sounding, but good advice in this thread, such as networking. Networking should not just be about meeting people who may be hiring, it's also about keeping a pulse on the industry and social engagement beyond just talking within online forums. Go to free conferences, meet people, engage. It makes it a lot easier to interview. Whatever you do, don't lie, and I recommend blocking anyone who recommend you do.

comments.author: marcus_holmes
comments.text: This is still the best article I've found on this subject: https://ludic.mataroa.blog/blog/ludics-guide-to-getting-soft... from one of my favourite bloggers, his other stuff is very worth reading. My take on it: the standard recruitment process is completely broken. Don't even start doing that. Sending applications to a job advert is an exercise in futility and will destroy your mental health. It's always about who you know. You have to go find people who are in a position to employ you, and impress them. This isn't difficult. They don't want to interview the stream of idiots that HR have approved any more than you want to jump through the hoops HR think are relevant. They want to employ someone who they know and like. So go to meetups, small business networking events, tech conventions, anything that will attract the kind of boss that you want to have. Talk to people. If you can, present something.

comments.author: rossy
comments.text: Like the weight space stuff, I think there's a small misdirection in how this is presented: Phrases like "write directly in machine code" seem to imply that ordinary LLMs intuitively understand machine code as just another language, like English or JavaScript, that they read from context and write directly as tokens, and that this intuitive understanding could mean increased efficiency or capabilities if you ask the LLM to just use the bytes rather than asking it to use the tools that human reverse engineers use. If that's what you assumed, the DeepSeek reasoning trace shatters that illusion. It's just disassembling by hand like what a human reverse engineer would do if you (sadistically?) denied them a disassembler. Yeah, the human reverse engineer would need an excellent memory of the x86_64 instruction reference, but we already know LLMs can recall a breadth of information. What we don't know, that this article also provides no evidence for, is if there will be any benefit in using the LLM for this over objdump. The article seems to intentionally conflate disassembly (computationally cheap) with decompilation (can be computationally expensive) to imply that there's some benefit to asking the LLM to work with machine code (seems impressive to the RE layman) rather than working in assembly (something you probably already assumed LLMs can do,) but the DeepSeek trace has a disassembly in it, and it's hard to imagine that inference will ever be cheaper or more reliable per-token than objdump is at producing the same output.

comments.author: whycombinetor
comments.text: Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket. From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

comments.author: nixpulvis
comments.text: I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision. More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams. Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.

comments.author: bikeshaving
comments.text: I’ve found that the “job” of using AI is mainly foible management. What the author describes here is a habit of coding agents to excessively use and create logging infrastructure, and sloppily leave it in production code even when unnecessary. For instance, I created an IPA IME keyboard ( https://ipabet.org/ ), and I found in review that Claude would leave the debugging tooling around unflagged, which essentially made the program a key-logger. These foibles come and go: early Claude Code refused to let programs crash, mangled all the comments in your codebase, and then one week you find that it insists on ending all functions with `Of` as in `layoutOf()`, `viewOf()`. Finding and mitigating these annoying habits becomes part of the job. Code review becomes articulating with this entity why certain patterns in the code are silly and should be changed. The author mentions performance and security issues as the domain of “the architect.” For performance, I’ve found that Claude Code has more or less solved this domain, and can profile and optimize code across a variety of stacks and languages using sophisticated, ad-hoc workflows. For security, it’s just an ever-ending nightmare where random habits and sloppy implementation create random vulernabilities, compounded by the fact that Anthropic has added “safeguard filters” whenever you naively say you’re looking for them. Nevertheless, I’m not sure the architecting role as they describe won’t be automated in the near future.

comments.author: ChrisMarshallNY
comments.text: > But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. In my case, I have been able to mitigate this. I have an LLM (ChatGPT, but I don't think it matters that much, anymore), that I load with vast amounts of information about the end-users of my apps. It generally makes excellent decisions, and often pushes back on my requests, if they may not deliver a good result. I sometimes think it knows more about my users than I do. One example, is that it does a very good job on translation. The feedback has been overwhelmingly positive. It blows away the stuff I used to have done by professional translation agencies. I still feel that I need to design the overall architecture, but I sometimes wonder if that's just because I'm a control freak.
